articles.title: It’s Been 25 Years Since 9/11—These Are the 10 Most Powerful Stories About the Tragedy
articles.content:
Twenty-five years goes by in an instant. On Sept. 11, 2001, four planes were hijacked and pointed directly at the heart of the country, and life hasn’t been the same since. Though time can have a dulling effect, pushing those memories into a safe corner of one’s mind or lengthening the time between them, the awful visuals and lived experiences never go away.
It’s hard to believe, but a third of Americans were born after 9/11. But the effects of the attack—an enhanced surveillance state, increased airport security and military incursions around the world—are felt by everyone. Universal, too, are the stories of heroism, friendship and sacrifice that will forever mark that sad day.
With the 25th anniversary of 9/11 upon us, we put together a list of some of the most important journalism that took us through the day as it happened or examined it from the perspective of time. Ahead, we have 10 remarkable stories about Sept. 11, 2001. Some have been celebrated for decades; others you may never have read.
Read on to look back at the tragedy and perhaps find hope in some of the stories.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, real stories, travel, tech and trending topics all week long.
On Sept. 12, 2001, the Associated Press published a photograph of an unknown man falling headfirst from the north tower of the World Trade Center. In 2003, Esquire journalist Tom Junod set out to determine who the man was by reviewing the entire series of 12 photographs taken by AP photographer Richard Drew. The result explores collective grief and trauma and has become one of the defining pieces of journalism from the post–9/11 era.
Read more at Esquire
The title of this piece refers to the amount of time that elapsed between the first plane hitting the north tower at 8:46 a.m. and its collapse at 10:28 a.m. Eight months after the attack, the New York Times published an accounting of those 102 minutes by piecing together emails and phone calls from those trapped and killed, as well as recollections from survivors. It’s as chilling now as it was when it was first published.
Read more at The New York Times
The staff of the Wall Street Journal won the Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Reporting in 2002 for its 9/11 coverage. That coverage included real-time reports of the planes and collapses as well as potential impacts, including to airport security and the economy, as they were happening. One particularly harrowing story is a first-person accounting of that day called “The Eye of the Storm: One Journey Through Desperation and Chaos,” by John Bussey.
You can read all of the winning coverage at the Pulitzer Prize page, below.
Read more at The Pulitzer Prizes
This narrative account, published just days after 9/11, weaves together events at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and the final moments of United Flight 93, which went down in Pennsylvania. David Maraniss reconstructs the day through survivor accounts and reporting that paint a vivid picture of the chaos and destruction, as well as how it was seen through the eyes of people living through it in real time.
Read more at The Washington Post
Jennifer Senior’s devastating account of one family’s loss after the attacks won the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for Feature Writing. Bobby McIlvaine was just 26 years old on Sept. 11, 2001, and the story of the different ways his family coped with losing their charming and ambitious son, brother and boyfriend reminds us that grief is unpredictable and personal.
Read more at The Atlantic
Rick Resorla, a former British paratrooper and U.S. Army veteran, was the head of security for Morgan Stanley in the south tower of the World Trade Center. Credited with saving thousands of people, he died when he went back inside to offer more help. This piece by James B. Stewart tells the story of that day through the lens of Resorla’s personal life before the attacks, as well as through his loved ones, who subsequently had to process his heroism and death.
Read more at The New Yorker
This story, published just weeks after 9/11, looks at the lives of five people who were affected by the attacks and how they dealt with the immediate aftermath. A priest delivers a mass, a widow gives her daughter a bath, a firefighter can’t stop thinking of falling bodies. It’s an intimate look at “five people out of the multitudes,” and it stays with you.
Read more at The Washington Post
Windows on the World was a celebrated restaurant at the top of the north tower, and when the first plane hit the building, all escape routes for the 170 employees and patrons who were there that morning were severed. This story, which won a James Beard Award for Best Personal Essay, is told by Cal Sussman, a writer who took a wine class and then became a sommelier at Windows on the World. It works through survivor’s grief and paints a touching portrait of a beloved New York City institution.
Read more at Esquire
Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark worked on the south tower’s 81st and 84th floors, respectively, and they are two of only four known survivors of the floors above the impact zone. Clark made the fateful decision to go down the only open stairwell, ignoring pleas from others to go up to the roof, and heard Praimnath calling for help. Both reached the ground floor and ran from the building just as it collapsed, and they are still friends to this day.
Read more at The Guardian
This comprehensive retrospective of the first minutes of the attack combines narrative text, photography, video and data journalism to tell the story of what was happening on the ground as the day unfolded. The 17 minutes refers to the time between the first plane hitting the north tower and the second hitting the south one, and reporter Garrett M. Graff highlights a range of accounts from regular people as well as military and government officials about the confusion of that day.
Read more at National Geographic
The post It’s Been 25 Years Since 9/11—These Are the 10 Most Powerful Stories About the Tragedy appeared first on Reader's Digest.

articles.title: You’ll Never Guess How the Football Huddle Got Its Start—Here’s the Fascinating History Behind This Strategy
articles.content:
I firmly believe that the only good thing about the end of summer is the beginning of football season. Though I’m a die-hard New York Giants fan (it’s been a rough few years, but things are gonna turn around!), I’ll watch any and every game I can. On Sundays—and Monday and Thursday nights—from Week 1 through the postseason, you’ll find me near a TV, very likely yelling at the announcers.
But even if the extent of your football knowledge is the name of the team your family roots for, you’ve seen the huddle: The action ends, the players wander back toward one another, and suddenly they’re standing shoulder to shoulder in a little circle. There’s some serious discussion, a few nods, and then they break apart and race to their positions.
It happens over and over, in every football game. It’s such a familiar part of the sport that most of us never stop to wonder about it. But why do football players huddle?
As it turns out, this football staple has a very distinct origin—and it’s one you’d likely never guess. For the deets on one of football’s most recognizable rituals, I turned to two experts: football historian Ken Crippen, founder of the Football Learning Academy, and Jon Kendle, vice president of Archives and Exhibits at the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
Whether you know a blitz from a nickel package or just enjoy the game (or the snacks), we guarantee that you’ll find this fascinating. Read on for the answer before kickoff.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, entertainment, humor, travel and tech.
The roots of American football trace back to both soccer and rugby, with the first college football game between Rutgers and Princeton in 1869. In the 1880s, Yale player and coach Walter Camp, who became known as the “father of American football,” helped establish rules that increasingly separated American football from rugby.
The game was barely recognizable by today’s standards. “When it first emerged, forward passing was illegal,” says Crippen. “You would see mass-momentum plays and a lot of physicality.”
And that physicality could be deadly. “So many players died on the field that they would have running counts in the newspapers,” he adds. Football was a game still figuring itself out, from how it was played to how teams communicated in the middle of it.
In the early days of football, quarterbacks simply called or signaled the play—often right at the line of scrimmage. Of course, this “was a problem because the defense could hear the play call,” Crippen notes.
Another option was to call the play while the team was approaching the line of scrimmage, “but far enough away that the defense could not hear them,” he says.
That created an obvious strategic problem: If the defense could hear the play call, it could adjust accordingly. Teams needed a way to communicate without giving away their plans.
The football huddle is widely credited to Gallaudet College, now Gallaudet University, a school for deaf students in Washington, D.C. Gallaudet’s football team was made up of deaf players who communicated using sign language, creating a unique challenge on the field.
Because their opponents were often schools for the hearing-impaired, Gallaudet quarterback Paul Hubbard worried they were watching his hands to read his team’s intentions, according to Kendle. Hubbard’s solution was to form a circle so opponents couldn’t read his signs.
That circle became the first football huddle. The exact game in which it debuted is unknown, but Crippen says the practice appears to have developed organically during Gallaudet’s 1894 season, when the team primarily played the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf and the New York School for the Deaf.
The huddle—which Kendle calls “a magical and special place of trust”—didn’t immediately become a universal part of football.
Amos Alonzo Stagg, one of the sport’s great early innovators, began using the huddle while coaching at the University of Chicago in 1896. But it took a while for the rest of football to catch on. “Stagg was an innovator, and whatever he did was usually copied by other college teams,” Crippen says. Still, the huddle “did not really catch on until the 1920s.”
But the huddle’s usefulness created a new problem: Teams could use it to waste time. “Some saw it as an intentional stall tactic,” Crippen says. That led to rules in the 1930s designed to keep teams from spending too much time in the huddle. Eventually, the introduction of the play clock in 1976 made those restrictions unnecessary. Today, the NFL gives offenses a set amount of time to begin the next play.
Here’s the funny thing: There’s no rule saying a football team needs to huddle. According to the current NFL Rulebook, “a huddle is the action of two or more players in the field of play or in the end zone who, instead of assuming their normal position for the snap, free kick or fair catch kick, form a group for receiving instructions for the next play or for any other reason.”
What happens inside that circle is up to the offense. In a typical huddle, the quarterback communicates instructions for the next play. That, notes Kendle, can “be for the formation, motions, snap count, blocking schemes, wide receiver routes and which gap the running back should run through.”
The huddle also gives the offense a moment to take stock. “It allows the team to see who is hurt, tired or seeing something that the offense can take advantage of against the defense,” Crippen says.
Kendle adds that the huddle can conceal the offense’s formation, making it more difficult for the defense to line up correctly before the snap.
Because sometimes the best way to beat a defense is to deny it time to respond. Enter the no-huddle offense: Rather than gathering to discuss the next play, the offense lines up immediately. The NFL describes it as a strategy that can conserve time, catch the defense off guard and prevent defensive substitutions.
In the 1980s and early 1990s, the Cincinnati Bengals and Buffalo Bills featured “no-huddle” offenses, according to Kendle. The Bills and their “hurry-up” offense advanced to four consecutive Super Bowls.
By the way: No-huddle football is hardly new. Crippen traces its use back to John Heisman (yes, the trophy is named for him), who used the offense at Auburn in 1899.
If the huddle was invented to make communication easier and more secretive, modern technology has made communicating plays much easier.
In the 1940s, Cleveland Browns coach Paul Brown used a “messenger guard” system, in which a substitute player could enter the game with the play from the sideline. Brown also experimented with radio headsets in the 1950s, though it wasn’t until 1994 that the NFL instituted radio helmets to allow limited communication from the sidelines to the quarterback on the field, according to Kendle.
Technology has continued to advance football communication. In 2023, Gallaudet University and AT&T debuted a 5G-connected football helmet that allowed a coach to select a play on a tablet and send it to a digital display inside the quarterback’s helmet.
Probably not—or, at least, not entirely.
“I believe the huddle is still an essential part of football,” Kendle says. “It allows the team to come together as a unit to receive critical instructions and make sure they are on the same page.”
So the next time you watch a football game and see the offense gather around their quarterback, take a second to appreciate what you’re actually looking at. The huddle may look like a simple pause between plays, but it’s one of football’s most enduring strategic tools—giving players a moment to communicate, regroup and figure out what comes next.
Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have a football game to watch.
The post You’ll Never Guess How the Football Huddle Got Its Start—Here’s the Fascinating History Behind This Strategy appeared first on Reader's Digest.

articles.title: Watch The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview with Author Ayad Akhtar
articles.content:
阿基德·艾亚德是一位不安于现状的作家。这位普利策戏剧奖得主兼小说家，在职业生涯中一直在探讨美国归属感和信仰最棘手的问题。他的处女作《美国德尔维什》讲述了一个穆斯林男孩在威斯康星州长大，与信仰和初恋抗争的故事。之后是《羞耻》，这部犀利的剧本描述了一位成功的巴基斯坦裔美国律师在一次爆炸性的晚餐派对中精心构建的生活开始崩溃。自此，阿基德探索了从宗教与家庭（《谁与什么》）到华尔街的过度（《垃圾》）再到地缘政治与资本主义（《看不见的手》）等各种主题。换句话说：如果有一个复杂的主题大多数人在晚餐时更愿意避谈，阿基德可能已经写出了一部关于它的杰作。

他赢得的荣誉证明了这一点。除了因《羞耻》获得普利策戏剧奖外，阿基德还两次获得托尼奖提名，他的2020年小说《祖国挽歌》——这部作品模糊了虚构与文化批评的界限——被《纽约时报》评为当年十大好书之一。六年后，阿基德以一部新小说重返，再次使作者与角色之间的界限变得诱人地难以分清。

他的最新作品《光辉》，将于9月29日出版，以一个惊人的前提开篇：一位名叫阿基德·艾亚德的成功小说家（没错，你读对了）在纽约上州的乡村道路上遭遇了意外撞击，并受了严重伤。但在这部自虚小说中，这起事故只是一个开始。"他经历了世界的某种颠覆，"阿基德说，"他的经历进入了一个非常奇怪、非常诡异、医学上可疑的领域，同时也是道德高尚、情感敏感的领域，他经历了一个非常困境的世界。"

在这期《读者文摘》电梯访谈中，雷·贝尔兹·雷与阿基德交谈了《光辉》、他作为小说家和剧作家的生活、塑造他的书籍和作家，以及许多其他内容。

在下面观看阿基德的独家访谈，然后向下滚动以发现他的书籍、备受赞誉的剧本和阅读推荐！

Ayad Akhtar is the kind of writer who refuses to play it safe. The Pulitzer Prize–winning playwright and novelist has spent his career tackling some of the thorniest questions about faith and what it means to belong in America. His debut novel, American Dervish, followed a Muslim boy growing up in Wisconsin and wrestling with faith and first love. Then came Disgraced, his blistering play about a successful Pakistani American lawyer whose carefully constructed life begins to unravel over the course of one explosive dinner party. Since then, Akhtar has taken on everything from religion and family (The Who & The What) to Wall Street excess (Junk) to geopolitics and capitalism (The Invisible Hand). In other words: If there’s a complicated subject most people would rather avoid at dinner, Akhtar has probably written something brilliant about it.

And he’s got the accolades to prove it. In addition to winning the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for Disgraced, Akhtar has received two Tony Award nominations, and his genre-bending 2020 novel, Homeland Elegies—which blurred the boundaries between fiction and cultural criticism—was named one of the 10 best books of the year by the New York Times. Now, six years later, Akhtar is returning with a novel that once again makes the line between author and character tantalizingly difficult to find.

His latest, The Radiance, out Sept. 29, begins with a startling premise: A successful novelist named Ayad Akhtar (yes, you read that right) is struck and severely injured in a hit-and-run on a country road in upstate New York. But the accident in this autofictional novel is only the beginning. “He experiences a kind of upending of his world,” says Akhtar, “as his experience veers into a very weird and uncanny, and medically questionable, as well as morally heightened, emotionally sensitive register, and he experiences a very fraught world around him.”

For this episode of the Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview, Leigh Belz Ray caught up with Akhtar to talk about The Radiance, his life as both a novelist and playwright, the books and writers that have shaped him and plenty more.

Watch the exclusive interview with Ayad Akhtar below, and then scroll down to discover his books, acclaimed plays and reading recommendations!

articles.title: The Jellycat Christmas Collection Just Dropped—and These Festive Plushies Won’t Last Long
articles.content:
虽然冬天尚未正式到来，但万圣节和感恩节仍然大放异彩。如果你属于那种喜欢提前准备节日购物的人（这样可以在12月减少一些压力），那么现在就是抢购圣诞礼物的黄金时机，尤其是当这些礼物还在库存的时候。此外，分散购物也能更好地保护你的钱包。

Jellycat这个备受喜爱的毛绒玩具品牌已经率先迎接节日的到来。2026年的圣诞系列已经上市，带来了许多节日风格的可爱产品。以下是你需要了解的一切。

今年的圣诞系列充满了软绵绵的冬季动物、节日主题的Amusables玩偶，以及你所期待的Jellycat特有的温馨圣诞魅力。和以往一样，这些毛绒玩具都是由高质量的面料制成，并且在道德劳动条件下生产。

2026年的新朋友包括：

几年前，我了解到许多（但不是全部）Jellycat玩偶“适合从出生时开始使用”，从那以后我就开始送给我的现在学步的孩子。不用说，这些玩偶非常受欢迎。它们非常柔软，经过几次真正的灾难性事故后，我也可以确认一些玩偶在洗衣机里洗涤后依然完好无损。

作为Jellycat的长期粉丝和收藏家，我也了解到这个品牌每年推出的设计有多少，以及其中有多少是限量版的。如果你发现一个你喜欢的玩偶在库存中，不要等太久下单，尤其是如果有一个新的小伙伴你（或你的孩子）绝对必须拥有的话。

Jellycat玩偶很少打折，但售罄的风险是真实的。以下是我今年冬季系列中希望抢购的产品。

我名单上最想要的是新款Ulrich Wolf。我的女儿迷上了Jellycat的Smudge系列，这个毛茸茸的朋友有着相同的令人难以抗拒的、软绵绵的外观，让这些玩偶如此难以放下。为了在冬天茁壮成长，Ulrich的厚实、蓬松的毛发让他整个赛季都非常舒适。

这个可爱的Mullover Spiced Drink已经准备好滑雪，配备雪镜。肉桂棒和橙子片从顶部探出，给这个小饮品增加了一份季节性的魅力。半是温馨的节日装饰，半是可爱的毛绒玩偶，这个充满滑雪小屋氛围的玩偶让人印象深刻。

我喜欢Fitswell Mitten和她的两个好朋友Perta Snow Boot和Pomilly的软柔冬季色彩搭配。它们简直是完美冬日场景的毛绒玩偶版本。Fitswell会成为雪地漫步、欣赏圣诞灯光或与一杯热可可一起舒适休闲的美好伙伴。

Munro Scottie Dog准备好了应对寒冷的天气，穿着节日风格的高领毛衣。他的冬季小装扮让这个已经可爱的小狗更加难以抗拒，我想象他蜷缩在圣诞树下的礼物中。

新款圣诞Jellycats将于9月9日在品牌官网首发。你还可以在其他零售店购买Jellycats，如Nordstrom和The Paper Store，但选择可能有所不同。

Yes, Halloween and Thanksgiving still have their moment in the spotlight before winter officially takes over. But if you’re the type who likes to get a head start on holiday shopping (and spare your December self a little stress), now is the perfect time to snag a few Christmas gifts while they’re still in stock. Plus, spreading out your shopping can be a whole lot kinder to your wallet.

Naturally, beloved plush brand Jellycat is already getting into the holiday spirit. The 2026 Christmas collection is already here, bringing plenty of festive cuteness. Here’s everything you need to know.

What is the 2026 Christmas Jellycat collection?

This year’s holiday collection is packed with cuddly winter creatures, festive Amusables, and all the cozy, Christmasy charm you’d expect from Jellycat. And as always, the beloved plush toys are made with high-quality fabrics under ethical working conditions.

The new friends for 2026 include:

  • Amuseables Mullover Spiced Drink
  • Amuseables Pomilly
  • Amuseables Perta Snow Boot
  • Amuseables Fitswell Mitten
  • Amuseables Silver Star
  • Ulrich Wolf
  • Bizzlestomp Bear
  • Munro Scottie Dog ‘Winter Jumper’
  • Tawoola Owl

My top picks

A few years ago, I learned that many (though not all) Jellycats are “suitable from birth,” and I’ve been gifting them to my now-toddler ever since. Needless to say, they’re a big hit. They’re incredibly soft, and after a few truly catastrophic messes, I can also confirm that some have survived a spin in the washing machine just fine.

As a longtime Jellycat fan and collector, I’ve also learned just how many designs the brand releases each year—and how many are only around for a limited time. If you spot one you love in stock, don’t wait too long to pounce, especially if there’s a new little pal you (or your kiddo) absolutely has to have.

Jellycats rarely go on sale, but the risk of selling out is very real. Here’s what I’m hoping to snag from this year’s winter collection.

Ulrich Wolf

Shop on Jellycat

At the top of my list is the new Ulrich Wolf. My daughter is obsessed with Jellycat’s Smudge collection, and this fuzzy friend has that same irresistible, floppy look that makes those plushies so hard to put down. Built to thrive in winter, Ulrich’s thick, shaggy fur makes him extra cozy for cuddles all season long.

Mullover Spiced Drink

Shop on Jellycat

This cheeky Mullover Spiced Drink is ready to hit the slopes, snowboarding goggles and all. Cinnamon sticks and orange slices peek out from the top, giving this little sipper an extra dose of seasonal charm. Half cozy holiday decor and half adorable plush pal, this one packs major ski lodge vibes.

Fitswell Mitten

Shop on Jellycat

I’m loving the soft, wintry color palette of Fitswell Mitten and her two BFFs, Perta Snow Boot and Pomilly. Together, they’re basically the plushie versions of a perfect winter day. Fitswell would make a sweet companion for snowy strolls, Christmas-light viewing, or cozying up with a cup of hot cocoa.

Munro Scottie Dog 'Winter Jumper'

Shop on Jellycat

Munro Scottie Dog is ready for chilly weather in his festive turtleneck sweater. His tiny winter-ready outfit makes this already-adorable pup even harder to resist, and I can already picture him nestled among the presents under the tree.

Where to buy

New Christmas Jellycats debut on the brand’s official website on September 9. You can also shop at other official retailers that stock Jellycats, such as Nordstrom and The Paper Store, but selection may vary

articles.title: Here’s the Science Behind the Sunday Scaries—And How to Banish Them So You Can Actually Enjoy Your Entire Weekend
articles.content:
### 周日焦虑的科学依据及应对方法

许多人在周日傍晚会感受到一种独特的焦虑，即所谓的“周日焦虑”（Sunday scaries）。根据矢桥广告公司2025年的一项调查，82%的全职美国员工经历过这种情绪，其中42%的人因焦虑失眠，35%的人出现头痛、紧张和疲劳等身体症状。

#### 为什么会产生周日焦虑？
马里兰大学心理学教授亚历山大·J·沙克曼（Alexander J. Shackman）博士研究恐惧与焦虑，他指出，轻微的周日焦虑可能有益处，帮助人们评估过去的成功与失败，计划未来一周的挑战。然而，当这种预备系统失控，开始占据整个周末时，问题就出现了。

周日焦虑的核心原因是**对比效应**。周六是周末的高峰，人们远离工作压力，而周二则已进入工作节奏。周日位于周末自由与工作责任的交界处，大脑察觉到这种转变，开始准备应对潜在的压力。

#### 大脑对压力的反应
沙克曼的研究团队在2025年《神经科学杂志》的fMRI扫描研究中发现，大脑对威胁预期（如周一的工作压力）会激活一个复杂的神经网络，包括**延展扁桃体**、**前岛回**和**中额回皮层**。这些区域协同工作，帮助人们组织应对危险的反应。

- **延展扁桃体**：在不确定威胁时保持更持久的活跃状态，解释了为何尚未发生的事仍能让人焦虑。
- **前额皮层**：帮助计划、决策和调节行为，但过度思考可能导致反复担忧而无解决方案。
- **前岛回和中额回皮层**：帮助大脑优先处理重要信息，但过度关注压力可能破坏周末的休息。

#### 焦虑如何影响身体？
压力会激活心血管系统，导致心率加快、血压升高，并释放激素。2022年《生理心理学》的研究发现，压力组人群的心血管反应更强烈。另一项研究发现，37%的大学生在考试前皮质醇水平上升，表明身体在事件发生前就已反应。

#### 如何应对周日焦虑？
1. **有限度地计划周一**：给自己一个短暂的时间窗口，规划下周的任务并记录下来，然后停止思考。研究表明，解决问题的思考不会导致疲劳，而情绪化的复盘则会。
2. **真正放松**：2022年的研究发现，周末真正放松能显著降低心理压力。做一些让你感到休息的事，如散步、健身或阅读。
3. **运动转移注意力**：沙克曼建议，运动能转移焦虑的能量，无需高强度，只要打破思维定式即可。
4. **设定边界**：避免反复查看邮箱，保护睡眠质量，因为提前抗压可能影响休息。

周日焦虑并非完全有害，但若影响生活，可考虑寻求专业帮助或调整工作环境。平衡预备与休息，让周末真正属于自己。
articles.summary:
It usually starts with one seemingly simple thought. Tomorrow is Monday.

One minute, you’re enjoying the last stretch of your weekend. The next, you’re mentally opening your inbox, rehearsing tomorrow’s meeting in your head and remembering those three things you swore you would deal with on Friday and somehow never got to. Your shoulders tense. Your stomach twists. The weekend was supposed to last until you were nestled in bed, but your brain is already sounding Monday morning’s alarm clock.

That familiar shift from relaxed to vaguely doomed is what people mean when they talk about the Sunday scaries. And if you’ve ever Googled “what are the Sunday scaries” while actively experiencing them, you’re far from alone.

In a 2025 survey by Adobe of 1,004 full-time U.S. employees, 82% said they had experienced the Sunday scaries. And it gets worse: 42% said they had lost sleep over them, and 35% reported physical symptoms such as headaches, tension and fatigue.

Despite the cute alliterative name, there is real science behind the feeling. And believe it or not, it’s not all bad news. In fact, Alexander J. Shackman, PhD, a University of Maryland psychology professor who studies fear and anxiety, says mild Sunday nerves may even be useful. “They’re a chance to take stock of the successes and failures of the recent past, size up the most important challenges in the week to come and plan accordingly,” he explains. The trouble begins when that preparation system stops helping and starts hijacking your day.

So how do you get your brain to cut that out? We’ve got the answer, of course! Read on to find out what’s going on when you get that telltale twinge of anxiety on Sundays—and how to combat it.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more science, life, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

What are the Sunday scaries, exactly?

The Sunday scaries are the dread, worry or uneasiness that can show up as your time off winds down and the next workweek gets closer. You might feel restless, irritable or distracted. Your thoughts may race through Monday’s schedule, and you may have trouble relaxing or falling asleep.

Why Sunday? Shackman says part of the answer may be contrast. Saturday is the weekend’s peak, baby! You’re riding the high of that Friday feeling, and you’re safely removed from work. On the other end of the spectrum, once you’ve hit Tuesday, you are already back in the rhythm of the week. Sunday sits at the uncomfortable border between weekend freedom and whatever responsibilities are waiting on the other side.

“It feels like you’re about to encounter something different, something potentially stressful or challenging,” he says. Your brain notices that shift and starts preparing.

What causes this anticipatory dread?

Anxiety is partly a preparation system. It pulls your attention toward possible problems so you can respond to them. That’s useful when there’s something concrete to prepare for, such as a deadline, presentation or difficult conversation.

Some weeks simply give that system more material. In Adobe’s 2025 survey, burnout was the most commonly reported trigger, cited by 55% of respondents. High workloads came next at 50%, followed by project deadlines and toxic work environments.

The response can also change, depending on how threatening a situation seems and whether you feel equipped to handle it. Shackman says the brain takes into account things like how likely a problem is and what options you have for coping with it. When the response becomes much bigger than the actual demands, it’s like an overly sensitive security system. Instead of helping you prepare, it keeps sounding the alarm.

What happens in your brain when you get the Sunday scaries?

There is no tiny “Monday” switch in your brain. Anticipating a possible threat recruits a network of interconnected regions that work together to prepare your mind and body.

In a 2025 study published in the Journal of Neuroscience and co-authored by Shackman, researchers used fMRI scans to study threat anticipation in 220 adults. Both certain and uncertain threats engaged a shared network that included the extended amygdala, anterior insula and midcingulate cortex. Here’s how it all breaks down.

The extended amygdala tracks possible threats

The extended amygdala, located at the base of the forebrain, includes structures involved in organizing responses to danger. In the study, this area remained more persistently active when people anticipated an uncertain threat.

That helps explain why something that has not happened yet can still feel urgent. Your brain does not have to wait for Monday morning to start monitoring what might go wrong.

The prefrontal cortex helps you plan

Shackman says parts of the prefrontal cortex are also involved in anticipating stress. This area helps with planning, decision-making and regulating behavior.

That can turn worry into useful action. You check your calendar, decide what needs your attention and move on. The problem is when planning turns into rumination and you keep circling the same fears without solving anything.

Your attention gets pulled toward the threat

The anterior insula and midcingulate cortex are also part of the threat-anticipation network identified in Shackman’s study. Together, these regions help your brain prioritize potentially important information.

“Emotionally charged stimuli—pain, threat, dangers and so on—hijack attention,” Shackman says. Helpful when actual danger is nearby. Less helpful when you are trying to enjoy your Sunday and your mind is already at work.

What else happens to your body when it goes into fight-or-flight mode?

Once your brain senses a challenge, the response can spread through your body. Stress activates systems that affect heart rate, blood pressure and stress hormones. In a 2022 study published in Psychophysiology, researchers randomly assigned 99 people to a stressful task or a control condition. The stress group showed higher cardiovascular responses, including changes in heart rate and blood pressure.

Your body can also react before the stressful event begins. A 2022 study published in Biological Psychology measured cortisol in 78 college students on a regular class day and on the day of an exam. About 37% showed a specifically anticipatory response, with cortisol peaking before the exam rather than afterward.

Sleep can take a hit too, according to other studies. That is one reason Sunday-night worrying can be so frustrating. You are trying to prepare for Monday while potentially making yourself more tired for it.

How can you break out of this pattern?

First, ask whether the anxiety is actually helping. If a few minutes of thinking about Monday leads to a plan and you feel better afterward, the system may be doing its job. If you routinely wake up on Sundays with your mind racing, cannot enjoy the day or lose sleep over work, Shackman says the response is no longer helping you prepare.

Sometimes the issue is not your coping strategy. “For some people, escaping the Sunday scaries might require looking for a new job or renegotiating the current one,” Shackman says. “After all, some jobs really are terrible.” If the anxiety is intense, persistent or interfering with your life, it is also worth talking with a health-care or mental-health professional.

What are some practical ways to feel calmer on Sundays?

Don’t worry—we have a plan! These tips will help you get your end-of-the-weekend anxiety under control.

Turn vague worrying into a concrete plan

Give yourself a short window to look at the week ahead, decide what actually needs your attention and write it down. Then stop. One recent study found that emotionally loaded work rumination was associated with greater fatigue, while problem-solving thoughts were not. A specific plan may help you move from repeatedly worrying about work to deciding what you can actually do about it.

Make room for actual relaxation

If Sunday becomes one long period of mentally preparing for work, you never really get the recovery part of the weekend. A 2022 study found that among Japanese teachers who entered the weekend with higher stress, greater weekend relaxation was associated with a larger reduction in psychological stress. Translation: Do something that actually feels restorative to you and treat it as part of the weekend, not time you should be using to get ahead.

Move your body

Shackman’s advice is refreshingly uncomplicated. “Go for a walk or, better yet, a run. Lift some weights. Sign up for a class at the gym or YMCA,” he suggests.

Exercise is not a universal cure, but it gives you something concrete to do with that restless energy and can help you shift your attention away from the worry loop. You don’t need a heroic workout either. The goal is to interrupt the pattern, not add another item to your list of things you failed to accomplish this weekend.

Protect your Sunday-night sleep

Give work thoughts a stopping point, especially if checking your inbox tends to generate five new things to worry about. The sleep research matters here because anticipating stress can affect sleep even before the stressful event occurs.

A little anticipation can be useful. But when your brain starts treating Monday like an emergency before Sunday is even over, the goal is not to eliminate every worried thought—it’s to give yourself enough space to prepare, then let the rest of the weekend belong to you.

Why trust us

At Reader’s Digest, we’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. For this piece on the Sunday scaries, Miranda Manier tapped her longtime experience as a journalist and health editor to ensure that all information is accurate and offers the best possible advice to readers. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date.
